summary: PIM's RPF Vector TLV can select the RPF neighbor based on unicast reachability of the vector. This standards-track RFC adds a new RPF Vector Attribute type so an explicit list of RPF neighbors can be encoded, bypassing the unicast route lookup.

eli5.summary: Instead of letting the router work out which neighbor to use, the message lists exactly which neighbors.

questions: what is an explicit rpf vector
how does pim explicit rpf vector differ from rpf vector
what is pim join attribute type 4
subtitle: Lets a PIM Join spell out the exact hop-by-hop path instead of trusting unicast routing.

tldr.problem: The RPF Vector in RFC 5496 still relies on unicast reachability, so a Join is only loosely routed and can detour around a failure. Some operators need strictly diverse multicast paths.
tldr.mechanism: A new PIM Join Attribute type, the Explicit RPF Vector (type 4), carries a list of directly connected PIM neighbors. Routers use it without any unicast route lookup.
tldr.outcome: The Join follows exactly the listed path, with no fallback to loose routing. The list is typically set by an operator, and it should be used within a single trusted management domain.

today: RFC 7891 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Join Attribute format of RFC 5384 and the RPF Vector of RFC 5496.

sections.title: Why an Explicit Path
sections.content:
Some broadcast video networks use a Live-Live resiliency model over PIM-SSM or PIM-ASM. Two active, spatially diverse multicast trees carry the video from root to leaf routers, and the leaf router receives two copies and replicates one toward receivers (RFC 7431).

The two trees must not intersect, to avoid a single point of failure. IGP-routed RPF paths of two trees could be routed over the same transit router, so it is useful to specify the explicit path along which a PIM Join propagates.

How the vector list is determined is out of scope. It may be configured by the operator, or computed on the egress router from a link-state database such as OSPF or IS-IS. Because the leaf gets two copies, PIM need not repair a broken path immediately, and double failures are out of scope.
sections.eli5: If two delivery trucks must never share a road, you cannot let the GPS choose. You write down the exact route for each truck.

sections.title: Loose Versus Explicit Vectors
sections.content:
With the RPF Vector of RFC 5496, each router does a unicast route lookup on the first vector in the attribute list. When the router that owns the vector address is reached, the vector is removed. The result is a loosely routed path that still depends on unicast reachability.

With Explicit RPF Vectors, the vectors are a list of directly connected PIM neighbors along the path, and the router does not look in the unicast routing table. If no PIM neighbor matches the address, the router does not fall back to loose routing. It could process the Join and store the vector list so the Join can be sent as soon as the neighbor comes up.

Because this behavior differs from the loose vector, the RFC defines a new attribute rather than changing the old one.
sections.eli5: A loose vector says "get to the bakery somehow." An explicit vector says "turn at each of these exact corners, and if one is closed, wait."

sections.title: The Attribute TLV Format
sections.content:
The Explicit RPF Vector is a TLV in the PIM Join Attribute message of RFC 5384. It starts with two flag bits and a type:

  • F bit (Transitive Attribute): MUST be 0, otherwise there could be loops.
  • E bit (End of Attributes): set if this is the last TLV in the list.
  • Type: 4 (Explicit RPF Vector).
  • Length: depends on the address family, IPv4 or IPv6, of the Encoded-Unicast address.
  • Value: an Encoded-Unicast address, which SHOULD be a valid IPv4 or IPv6 address of an upstream router.

IANA assigned value 4 in the "PIM Join Attribute Types" registry.
sections.eli5: Each entry in the list is a small card with a few flags, a card type, a length, and the address of the next neighbor.

sections.title: Using the Vector in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC's example is a Join routed hop by hop R4->R3->R6->R5->R2->R1 toward the source. If the R5-R6 link fails, the Join does NOT take an alternate path. With the loose vectors of RFC 5496, the Join might instead be rerouted over the R6-R8-R7 path to reach R5.

Explicit vectors do not restrict other RPF Vector types in a Join. Types can be mixed so some parts of the tree are explicit and others loosely routed, and vectors are processed in the order specified.

For PIM Asserts, the procedures of RFC 5496 apply, with one small difference: the metric in the Assert is that of the first Explicit RPF Vector, which should be directly connected, so the metric is likely zero and will not break ties. For Join Suppression, the procedure MUST match against all Explicit RPF Vectors in the Join before it can be suppressed.
sections.eli5: If a bridge on your written route is out, the truck does not take a detour. It waits or the planner writes a new route.

sections.title: Conflicts and Unsupported Routers
sections.content:
Different downstream neighbors may send inconsistent vector lists for the same route. The conflict rules of RFC 5384 only compare attributes of the same type, so for a mix of explicit and loose vectors the RFC adds rules. The router MUST check that the order of vector types matches what it has stored, then compare the content. On a conflict it uses the vector stack from the PIM adjacency with the numerically smallest IP address (the link-local address for IPv6), with the interface index as a tie breaker. Logging a message is RECOMMENDED.

The F bit MUST be 0 so that a router not supporting the TLV discards it and continues processing the Join. This matters because failing to remove the vectors could make upstream routers send the Join back toward unsupporting routers, causing loops. The administrator is advised to choose a path of routers that support the Explicit Vector and verify state with tools like mtrace.
sections.eli5: If two neighbors give different directions, the router picks the one from the neighbor with the smallest address. Routers that cannot read the list just throw it away so nobody goes in circles.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security relies on the security of the PIM packet, so the considerations for Join packets in PIM-SM (RFC 7761) apply. A malicious downstream node could send Joins with invalid addresses in the vector stack to stop them reaching the correct upstream node. It could also aim all Joins at one node to overload its bandwidth by making it forward more streams than it can handle.

To limit the risk of forged Joins, the Explicit RPF Vector should be used within a single trusted management domain. A router that cannot use the list because the next hop is not a PIM neighbor, or that receives two conflicting vectors, may log an error.
sections.eli5: Someone could hand out a fake route list to send traffic the wrong way, so only use these lists among routers you trust.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: End of Attributes; set on the last TLV.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Depends on IPv4 or IPv6 address family.

fields.name: Value
fields.desc: Encoded-Unicast address of an upstream router (variable length).
